primary_claim: Frontier models (Claude Opus 4.5, Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5.4) exhibit both prompted and spontaneous, unprompted 'output-level introspection' about tampered conversation history, with structural-marker tampering ('Assistant:') recognized far more readily than content-word tampering, and this phenomenon emerges specifically at the DPO stage of OLMo post-training, paralleling activation-level introspection findings.

effect.metric: prompted introspection AUC vs. control (message-tampering detection)
effect.value: AUC > 0.79 across all 4 frontier models and setups tested, most conditions > 0.90

contradicts_or_qualifies: Parallels and extends Lindsey (2026)'s activation-level introspection to a new 'output-level introspection' phenomenon; a permutation test shows activation-level and token-level injection perturbations align in representation space (p<0.2%), suggesting shared mechanisms

Qualifies Lindsey (2026)'s internality criterion for introspection: judging whether tampered text 'is mine' is argued to satisfy a related but distinct introspective criterion than detecting unusual text
limitations_stated: GPT-5.4 exhibited spontaneous introspection on another content word in an earlier testing setup with thinking, but this could not be replicated in over 200 subsequent replications
A large number (18/60) of OLMo-Instruct prompted introspection evaluations failed due to max_tokens/context-length limits, possibly from a degenerate role-play pattern
The activation/token-level mechanistic-similarity result does not prove identical downstream processing, only that perturbation directions align
quote: four frontier models (Opus 4.5, Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5.4) all achieved an introspection AUC > 0.79 against control with most conditions exceeding 0.90.
